definition: Technology that lets computers do things that normally need human thinking, like understanding language, recognizing images, or making decisions.
everydayExample: The autocorrect on your phone and the recommendations on a streaming app are both small, everyday examples of AI.
whyItMatters: AI is showing up in more products every year, from search engines to customer service, so understanding the basic idea helps you make sense of the news.

definition: A way of building AI where a computer learns patterns from examples instead of being given step-by-step instructions by a programmer.
everydayExample: An email app that learns to flag spam by studying thousands of past emails, rather than following a fixed list of rules.
whyItMatters: Most modern AI, including chatbots and image generators, is built using machine learning, so it's the foundation for almost everything else in this glossary.

definition: A type of machine learning that uses many layers of connected calculations, loosely inspired by how neurons in the brain pass signals, to find patterns in large amounts of data.
everydayExample: The technology behind a phone camera automatically recognizing faces in a photo.
whyItMatters: Deep learning is what made today's most capable AI, including chatbots and image generators, possible.

definition: A computer system made of many simple, connected parts that work together to recognize patterns, loosely modeled on how brain cells connect to each other.
everydayExample: A neural network can learn to tell cats apart from dogs in photos after seeing thousands of labeled examples.
whyItMatters: Neural networks are the basic building block underneath nearly all modern AI systems.

definition: AI that creates new content, like text, images, audio, or video, instead of just analyzing or sorting existing content.
everydayExample: Typing a description and getting back an original image, or asking a chatbot to draft an email for you.
whyItMatters: Generative AI is behind most of the AI tools people use today, including chatbots, image generators, and writing assistants.

definition: A type of AI trained on huge amounts of text so it can understand and generate human-like language.
everydayExample: The AI behind chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all large language models.
whyItMatters: Large language models power most of today's AI writing tools, chatbots, and search assistants.

definition: An AI system that can work toward a goal and use tools to complete tasks, sometimes without needing step-by-step instructions.
everydayExample: An AI assistant that checks your calendar, finds available meeting times, and drafts an invitation on its own.
whyItMatters: AI agents can help people automate tasks that would otherwise require several manual steps.

definition: The text, question, or instruction you give an AI system to tell it what you want it to do.
everydayExample: Typing "Summarize this email in two sentences" into a chatbot is a prompt.
whyItMatters: How you phrase a prompt can change the quality of an AI's response, which is why prompt writing has become its own skill.

definition: The practice of carefully wording instructions to an AI system to get better, more accurate, or more useful results.
everydayExample: Adding "explain this as if I'm a beginner" to a question often gets a clearer answer from a chatbot.
whyItMatters: Good prompt engineering can make the same AI tool noticeably more useful without any technical changes.

definition: Small pieces of text, often parts of words, that an AI language model reads and generates one at a time.
everydayExample: The word "unbelievable" might be broken into three tokens: "un", "believ", and "able".
whyItMatters: AI tools often charge by the token and have limits on how many tokens they can handle at once, which affects cost and performance.

definition: Taking an already-trained AI model and training it further on a smaller, specific set of data so it gets better at a particular task.
everydayExample: Fine-tuning a general chatbot on a company's support documents so it can answer customer questions more accurately.
whyItMatters: Fine-tuning lets companies customize powerful AI models for their own needs without building one from scratch.

definition: The process of an already-trained AI model actually being used to produce an answer, as opposed to the earlier process of training it.
everydayExample: Every time you send a message to a chatbot and get a reply, that reply was produced through inference.
whyItMatters: Inference is what happens every time you use an AI tool, and its speed and cost affect how AI products feel to use.

definition: AI that can understand or create more than one type of content at once, such as text, images, audio, or video together.
everydayExample: An AI app that can look at a photo of a receipt and answer written questions about it.
whyItMatters: Multimodal AI lets tools understand the world more like people do, by combining different kinds of information.

definition: A technique where an AI model looks up relevant information from an outside source before answering, instead of relying only on what it memorized during training.
everydayExample: A chatbot that searches a company's internal documents before answering a question about company policy.
whyItMatters: This technique helps AI give more accurate, up-to-date answers and reduces made-up information.

definition: When an AI system confidently states information that is false, made up, or not actually supported by its sources.
everydayExample: A chatbot inventing a book title and author that don't actually exist, while sounding completely certain.
whyItMatters: Hallucinations are a key reason experts recommend double-checking important facts an AI gives you.

definition: The branch of AI focused on helping computers understand, interpret, and generate human language.
everydayExample: Voice assistants understanding spoken questions, or email apps detecting the tone of a message.
whyItMatters: Natural language processing is the foundation that makes chatbots, translation tools, and voice assistants possible.

definition: The branch of AI focused on helping computers understand and interpret images and video.
everydayExample: A phone unlocking itself after recognizing your face, or a self-checkout kiosk identifying produce by sight.
whyItMatters: Computer vision powers everything from medical scan analysis to self-driving car safety systems.

definition: The process of feeding an AI system large amounts of data so it can learn patterns and improve at a task.
everydayExample: Showing an AI millions of labeled photos of animals so it learns to identify a cat versus a dog.
whyItMatters: Training determines how capable, accurate, and safe an AI model ultimately is.

definition: AI models or tools whose underlying code or weights are shared publicly, so anyone can inspect, use, or build on them.
everydayExample: A developer downloading a freely published AI model to run on their own computer instead of paying for access to a closed one.
whyItMatters: Open-source AI can make powerful tools more accessible, but it also raises new questions about safety and misuse.

definition: A type of neural network design, introduced in 2017, that is especially good at understanding relationships between words in a sentence, no matter how far apart they are.
everydayExample: Transformers are the underlying architecture used in nearly every major chatbot today.
whyItMatters: The transformer design is the technical breakthrough behind the rapid progress in AI language tools since the late 2010s.

definition: A way of turning words, sentences, or images into lists of numbers that capture their meaning, so a computer can compare how similar two things are.
everydayExample: A search tool that finds "laptop bag" results when you search "computer sleeve", because their embeddings are close in meaning.
whyItMatters: Embeddings are what let AI search and recommendation tools understand meaning instead of just matching exact words.

definition: A large, general-purpose AI model trained on broad data, which can then be adapted or fine-tuned for many different specific tasks.
everydayExample: A single large model that can be adapted to write emails, summarize documents, or answer customer questions.
whyItMatters: Foundation models let companies build many different AI products from one underlying system instead of starting from scratch each time.

definition: The amount of text an AI model can consider at one time when generating a response, measured in tokens.
everydayExample: If you paste a very long document into a chatbot and it forgets the beginning, you've likely gone past its context window.
whyItMatters: A larger context window lets an AI handle longer documents and conversations without losing track of earlier details.

definition: The internal numerical settings a neural network adjusts during training; roughly, the "knowledge dials" that get tuned as the model learns.
everydayExample: A model described as having "70 billion parameters" has that many internal values shaping how it responds.
whyItMatters: Parameter count is one rough indicator of a model's scale and potential capability, though not the only one.

definition: A type of generative AI that creates images by starting with random noise and gradually refining it into a clear picture, step by step.
everydayExample: AI image generators that turn a text description into a picture typically use diffusion models.
whyItMatters: Diffusion models are the main technology behind today's most popular AI image and video generators.

definition: An AI model's ability to call external programs, like a calculator, search engine, or calendar app, to complete a task more reliably.
everydayExample: A chatbot that uses a live web search tool to answer a question about today's weather instead of guessing.
whyItMatters: Tool use lets AI models go beyond their training data and interact with real, current information and systems.

definition: AI systems designed to take actions and make decisions on their own, with little or no step-by-step human guidance.
everydayExample: A self-driving car making moment-to-moment steering and braking decisions without a person directing each one.
whyItMatters: The more autonomy an AI system has, the more important it becomes to test its safety and reliability carefully.

definition: The field focused on making sure AI systems behave reliably, avoid causing harm, and stay aligned with what people actually want.
everydayExample: Testing a chatbot extensively before release to make sure it won't give dangerous instructions if asked.
whyItMatters: As AI systems become more capable and widely used, AI safety research helps reduce real-world risks.

definition: The effort to make sure an AI system's goals and behavior actually match what its human users and developers intend.
everydayExample: Training a chatbot to refuse harmful requests even if a user tries to trick it into ignoring its guidelines.
whyItMatters: Poor alignment can cause AI to behave in unexpected or unwanted ways, even if it's technically working as designed.

definition: A training method where human reviewers rate an AI's responses, and the model is adjusted to produce more of the highly-rated answers.
everydayExample: People ranking which of two chatbot replies is more helpful, and the model learning from those rankings.
whyItMatters: This technique is a major reason modern chatbots feel more helpful and conversational than earlier AI systems.

definition: When an AI system produces unfair or skewed results because of patterns, gaps, or imbalances in the data it was trained on.
everydayExample: A hiring tool that unfairly favors certain resumes because its training data reflected past, biased hiring decisions.
whyItMatters: Bias can cause real harm when AI is used in sensitive areas like hiring, lending, or healthcare.

definition: A large collection of information, like text, images, or numbers, that is used to train or test an AI model.
everydayExample: A collection of millions of labeled photos used to train an AI to recognize street signs.
whyItMatters: The quality and diversity of a dataset strongly shapes how accurate and fair an AI system turns out to be.

definition: A set of step-by-step instructions a computer follows to solve a problem or complete a task.
everydayExample: The ranking system a social media app uses to decide which posts to show you first.
whyItMatters: Nearly all software, including AI, is built from algorithms, so the word comes up constantly in tech news.

definition: A defined way for one piece of software to request information or services from another, like a menu of actions one program offers to others.
everydayExample: A weather app pulling live forecast data from a weather service through an API, instead of collecting the data itself.
whyItMatters: Most AI tools are accessed by developers through an API, which is how AI features end up inside other apps.

definition: A software program designed to hold a conversation with a person, often using text or voice.
everydayExample: Customer service widgets on websites that answer basic questions before connecting you to a human.
whyItMatters: Chatbots are one of the most common, everyday ways people directly interact with AI today.

definition: An AI technique that determines whether a piece of text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral feeling.
everydayExample: A company scanning thousands of product reviews to see whether customers are generally happy or unhappy.
whyItMatters: Sentiment analysis helps businesses and researchers quickly understand large amounts of text-based opinion.

definition: The field that combines engineering and AI to build physical machines that can sense their surroundings and act in the real world.
everydayExample: A warehouse robot that uses AI-powered vision to pick specific items off a shelf.
whyItMatters: Pairing AI with robotics is extending automation from screens into physical tasks like manufacturing and logistics.

definition: A specialized database that stores embeddings so an AI system can quickly search for the most similar pieces of information by meaning, not just exact text matches.
everydayExample: A customer support tool that instantly finds the most relevant help article for a question, even if the wording doesn't match exactly.
whyItMatters: Vector databases are a key piece of infrastructure behind many retrieval-augmented AI tools.

definition: The specific numerical values a neural network learns during training; downloading a model's weights means downloading its learned knowledge.
everydayExample: When developers talk about "open-weight" models, they mean the trained numerical values are available for anyone to download and run.
whyItMatters: Access to model weights determines whether a model can be run independently, inspected, or modified by outside developers.

definition: A technique that lets an AI model weigh which parts of the input are most relevant when producing each part of its output.
everydayExample: When translating a long sentence, an attention mechanism helps the model focus on the specific words that matter most for each translated word.
whyItMatters: Attention is the core idea that makes transformer-based models so good at understanding context in long passages.

definition: Running AI models directly on a local device, like a phone or camera, instead of sending data to a remote server.
everydayExample: A phone's camera app recognizing faces for autofocus without sending any photos to the internet.
whyItMatters: Edge AI can be faster and more private, since data doesn't have to travel to and from a distant server.

definition: Artificially generated data, created by a computer rather than collected from real-world events, used to train or test AI models.
everydayExample: Generating thousands of simulated road scenes to help train a self-driving car's AI without needing that many real drives.
whyItMatters: Synthetic data can fill gaps where real data is scarce, expensive, or sensitive to collect.

definition: Laws and government rules that set requirements or limits on how AI systems can be built, sold, or used.
everydayExample: A law requiring companies to disclose when a photo or video was generated or altered by AI.
whyItMatters: Regulation shapes what AI companies are allowed to build and how much transparency the public gets about AI systems.

definition: An AI assistant built into a piece of software to help a person complete tasks faster, while the person stays in control.
everydayExample: An AI feature inside a spreadsheet app that suggests formulas or summarizes a table when asked.
whyItMatters: Copilot-style tools are one of the most common ways everyday software is adding AI features for work.

definition: A large facility packed with computer servers, used to store data and run large-scale computing tasks, including training and running AI models.
everydayExample: When a company announces a new multi-billion-dollar data center, it's building the physical infrastructure its AI systems actually run on.
whyItMatters: The massive data center construction boom driven by AI is reshaping energy use, local economies, and environmental debates worldwide.
